title: The Battle Before The Battle
subtitle: Rules vs. People
tagline: A rule can be consistently enforced and still be wrongly applied.
headline: Rules vs. People
headline_sub: When the Policy Matters More Than the Person
seo_title: Rules vs. People: When Policy Matters More Than Person
seo_description: Following the rule isn’t always doing right. Jesus, the Sabbath and the man with the withered hand: how leaders keep policy from replacing wisdom and mercy.
og_image_alt: Rules vs. People: A rule can be consistently enforced and still be wrongly applied. TheWrkShop, Leadership & Culture.

scriptures.text: Then he said to them, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.”

Then Jesus asked them, “Which is lawful on the Sabbath: to do good or to do evil, to save life or to kill?” But they remained silent. He looked around at them in anger and, deeply distressed at their stubborn hearts, said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.”

blocks.text: Picture the room.
A man needs healing.
Jesus sees him.
The religious leaders see him.
But they are looking for different things.

items: Jesus sees someone to restore.
His opponents see an opportunity to accuse.

blocks.text: The same person becomes the center of two completely different priorities.
The religious leaders are watching Jesus closely.
Not because they hope the man will be healed.
Because they want grounds for an accusation.
Then Jesus asks a question that exposes the contradiction beneath their reading of the rules:
Is the Sabbath a reason to withhold good?
Mark tells us Jesus is angry and deeply distressed by their stubborn hearts.
Don’t miss that.
A PERSON IS SUFFERING WHILE RELIGIOUS OBSERVERS ARE MORE CONCERNED WITH DEFENDING THEIR POSITION.
“IF WE FOLLOWED THE RULE, WE DID THE RIGHT THING.”
Not necessarily.
Imagine an employee facing a serious family emergency.
A manager has the discretion to help, but refuses even to consider it.
Why?
Because exercising judgment requires responsibility.
Or imagine someone seeking pastoral care.
They are redirected again and again because their situation doesn’t fit the established process.
Everyone follows the procedure.
Nobody meaningfully addresses the need.

items: The system functions.
The person suffers.

blocks.text: Why might leaders hide behind policies?

items: Fear of precedent.
Fear of criticism.
Fear of losing control.
Fear of making the wrong decision.
A preference for certainty.

blocks.text: Sometimes rules genuinely protect people from favoritism, abuse, or inconsistent treatment.
We should never confuse compassion with permission to ignore necessary safeguards.
But we must ask:
AM I PROTECTING THIS BOUNDARY BECAUSE IT IS RIGHT, OR BECAUSE EXAMINING IT MAKES ME UNCOMFORTABLE?
That’s the upstream battle.
The decision may look procedural.
But beneath it may be fear, avoidance, or misplaced loyalty to a system.
GOD’S COMMANDS ARE NOT THE ENEMY OF HUMAN FLOURISHING.
Jesus isn’t dismissing God’s law.
He is exposing a reading of it that buries its intended good.
“The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.”
That doesn’t make every human desire the measure of righteousness.
It reminds us that God’s commands are wise and good.
Our policies, however, are human instruments.
They must be examined.
A healthy institution needs both principled boundaries and wise discernment.

items: Rules without wisdom become mechanical.
Compassion without accountability can become arbitrary.

blocks.text: Faithful leadership requires both.

items: What rule are we defending without asking whether it still serves its purpose?
Who is affected by how we apply it?
What legitimate good does it protect?
Where have we confused consistency with righteousness?
Are we willing to examine exceptions fairly rather than simply rejecting difficult situations?
Would Jesus recognize the people our policies claim to serve?

blocks.text: Choose one policy that repeatedly creates hardship.

items: Understand why it exists.
Listen to those affected.
Identify the safeguards it legitimately provides.

blocks.text: Then examine whether the way you apply it is necessary, fair, and compassionate.
This works at home too. Is there a house rule you enforce to keep control rather than to protect and grow your kids?
Don’t abandon wisdom.
Restore purpose.
A rule can be consistently enforced and still be wrongly applied.

Father, give me courage to uphold what is right without becoming hardened toward people. Expose where I hide behind procedure to avoid responsibility. Teach me to protect others with wisdom, fairness, and compassion. Keep my heart attentive to those standing in front of me. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
The system can function while the person suffers.
Consistency alone does not establish righteousness.
The battle begins with what we believe the rule is protecting.
Never defend a process so fiercely that you forget its purpose.
—TheWrkShop
